subject: accountancy
book: Financial Accounting Part I; Financial Accounting Part II (NCERT, rationalised)

concepts.text: Accounting defined as identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information of an organisation to its users
Identifying: deciding which events are financial transactions worth recording
Measuring: expressing transactions in money terms (rupees) only
Recording: entering transactions chronologically in books, then classifying and summarising them
Communicating: presenting summarised information (reports, statements) to users in a usable form
Book-keeping versus accounting: book-keeping is the recording stage; accounting adds summarising, analysing and interpreting
Accounting as an information system that collects, processes and reports financial data to decision makers

sections.name: 1.2 Accounting as a Source of Information

concepts.text: Accounting information is the language of business used for economic decisions
Internal users: owners, management, employees and their needs
External users: investors, lenders/banks, creditors/suppliers, government and tax authorities, customers, researchers, public

Qualitative characteristic: reliability (verifiable, faithful, free from error and bias)

Calculating profit or loss for a period by matching revenues and expenses
Depicting financial position (assets and liabilities) through a balance sheet
Providing accounting information to various users for decision making
Accounting as the language of business and a historical record
Role as a current economic reality, an information system and a service activity
Limitations of accounting: ignores non-monetary facts, uses estimates and historical cost, affected by price-level changes and personal judgement
Entity and business transaction (exchange of money value between parties)
Assets: resources owned/controlled with future benefit; non-current (fixed) vs current assets
Liabilities: amounts owed to outsiders; non-current (long-term) vs current liabilities
Capital: owner's investment / owner's claim on assets
Sales and revenue: sales from ordinary goods/services; revenues include commission, interest, rent, dividend
Expense vs expenditure: cost used up in earning revenue vs spending whose benefit may last longer (capital vs revenue expenditure)
Profit (excess of revenue over expenses), gain (from incidental events, e.g. sale of fixed asset) and loss
Discount: trade discount (off list price) vs cash discount (for prompt payment)
Voucher as documentary evidence supporting a transaction
Goods, purchases (cash and credit) and stock/inventory (opening and closing)
Drawings: cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use

sections.name: Introduction: need for a theory base

concepts.text: Why uniform rules are needed: inter-firm and inter-period comparison and reliability of statements

Business entity concept: business is separate from its owner; capital shown as liability to owner
Money measurement concept: only money-measurable transactions recorded; problem of changing money value
Going concern concept: business assumed to continue indefinitely; basis for depreciation and asset classification
Accounting period concept: results measured for fixed intervals (financial year April-March, interim/quarterly)
Cost concept: assets recorded at acquisition cost including installation, freight; historical cost and its limitation
Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two effects; accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Revenue recognition (realisation) concept: revenue recorded when the right to receive arises, not on cash receipt
Matching concept: expenses of a period matched with revenues of the same period (outstanding/prepaid follow from it)
Full disclosure concept: all material information disclosed, including notes and footnotes
Consistency concept: same methods used period to period (e.g. stock valuation, depreciation)
Conservatism (prudence) concept: anticipate no profit, provide for all possible losses; stock at lower of cost or market; avoid secret reserves
Materiality concept: significant items disclosed separately; small items may be expensed
Objectivity concept: transactions backed by verifiable evidence free from personal bias
Exercise type: identify the concept applied/violated in a given situation (case-based activity)
Double entry system: both aspects recorded; complete, checks arithmetic accuracy through trial balance
Single entry system: incomplete records, mostly personal accounts and cash book; used by small traders
